title: Test the measuring instrument before judging the contestant.
evidence_kind: Retained historical game-observation and trial-result records; no new game run for this case study.

re_evaluation.target_rule: Each measured window must meet both frozen delivery targets.

relationship.instrument_difference: The save-building adapter and agent-tool implementation changed; the recorded evaluator identity changed.
relationship.interpretation: Same design and targets, rebuilt under a repaired instrument. This is not an identical-binary or identical-protocol performance comparison.

important_limits: A failed positive control prevented a contestant verdict; its missing measurements are null, not zero.
Disconnected control delivery of zero is the expected result, even though the delivery-target scorer labels that control FAIL.
The failed contestant produced both outputs. Failure means it missed the minimum in at least one required window, not that the factory never worked.
Recorded rates and outcomes for this case are from 9 September 2026 and were not rerun. Later outcomes are summarized in later_summary, each with its own date and limits.
This case is not a model ranking, a broad factory-design success claim or an earned-progression result.

The diagrams and tables are authored explanations. No game saves, map tiles, game asset tables, application source or private operational details are included. The page also shows images of the game in its walkthrough and progress section; they are not part of this measurement record.
Control windows lasted 61 game seconds; contestant windows lasted 121, 122 and 121 game seconds. They are different checks, not matched performance runs.

date_basis: All dates are UTC, as in the run records.

designer.model_note: Not named. The only record of the agent's model is private session data, and no public source confirms it.
designer.context: Started with a fresh context and was given only the challenge and the tools every contestant gets. The record shows its design used only those tools.
designer.choices: Selected copper and limestone deposits on the map and built routes to the central depot.
designer.instructions: Written for this run by the AI agent coordinating the work, not a frozen briefing. The result stands alone and is not compared with any other run.

measurement_conditions.request: Across the map, build a factory producing 20 copper ingots per minute and 15 concrete per minute.
measurement_conditions.note: Recorded contestant windows ran 121, 122 and 121 game seconds; each rate is divided by the recorded game time.

depot_checkpoints.note: Depot totals at each window boundary of the repaired trial. Each window rate is the change divided by the window length: copper window 1 is 32 ingots in 121 game seconds, and concrete window 3 is 30 in 121.

instrument_repair.fault: In the first trial the save-building adapter filled in a storage filter that the game leaves empty in its own saves. The control's materials reached the belts, but the depot counted none.
instrument_repair.fix: The adapter now writes the filter the way the game does. After the fix the known-flow control delivered both materials and the disconnected control delivered nothing.

miss_analysis.copper_window_1: No copper had reached the depot when measuring began (0 ingots at 181 game seconds). The trial record says the shortfall, followed by 60 a minute, is consistent with copper still traveling the long route when measuring began. That cause is not proven.
miss_analysis.concrete_window_3: The design used one concrete constructor. At normal speed the concrete recipe makes 15 a minute, the target itself, and this challenge offered no way to run a machine faster, so there was no margin. Window 3 delivered 30 concrete in 121 game seconds, where the target required 30.25.

later_finding_warmup.finding: The default 180-second warmup left three reference designs, built to pass their own library challenges, short in their first window: 9.23 of 30, 59.6 of 60 and 0.00 of 60 items a minute.
later_finding_warmup.change: Challenges in SaveBench's curated library now declare their own warmup; other challenges can still use the 180-second default. After the change, the first of those reference designs passed every window.
later_finding_warmup.effect_on_this_case: Not rescored. The FAIL stands as recorded, and the warmup explanation for its first copper window remains unproven.

earlier_passes_note: Factories designed by AI models passed smaller challenges on 8 and 9 September 2026, some of them before this case's FAIL was recorded. They are separate individual results and are not compared here.

credits.what: The save-building adapter is a narrow wrapper over a pinned copy of Satisfactory Agent Tools by petehunt, which is a fork of GreyHak's sat_sav_parse. Both projects are licensed GPL-3.0.

later_summary.what: A harder challenge: 120 copper ingots and 60 concrete a minute in each of three windows after a 180-second warmup, with Mk1 belts only.
later_summary.outcome: FAIL for every measured design by an AI model.
later_summary.limits: The FAILs were kept as recorded, and a version allowing a faster belt tier became a separate challenge.

later_summary.what: The same targets and warmup as a separate challenge that allowed a faster belt tier (Mk3).
later_summary.outcome: On 13 September, PASS in every window for designs by Claude Opus 4.7 (as configured; the same contestant setup reported that model when it ran later sessions) and GPT-5.5 (as configured). Claude's first pass on this challenge came from its own revision after a measured FAIL. Both contestants also had FAILs in these comparisons.
later_summary.limits: The software changed between comparisons and the contestants ran different numbers of trials, so this is not a ranking. Independent acceptance testing of the interface was not completed.

later_summary.what: A campaign in a persistent world, each session continuing from the one before, with declared starting stock and judged by milestones bought in the game.
later_summary.outcome: Claude Opus 4.7 (as its runtime reported) bought eight milestones.
later_summary.limits: The interface changed between sessions, so these are not scores on a fixed instrument. While those milestones were bought, the interface let the contestant move items into and out of machines without spending game time.

later_summary.what: Zach Stern decided that SaveBench measures factory design, tested by a production quota the factory must keep meeting through a hands-off period.

public_reference.title: Factorio Learning Environment
public_reference.authors: Jack Hopkins, Mart Bakler, Akbir Khan
public_reference.relevant_text: After every agent step, the throughput of the created structure is evaluated throughout a 60 second holdout period in-game

later_summary.what: The quota test: 30 wire a minute into a declared depot, counted only after the factory has been left untouched for a set period.
later_summary.contestant: Cursor's Auto setting. The records do not show which model it used.
later_summary.outcome: No session passed. The outcomes on record, for the first and fourth sessions, were INCONCLUSIVE because the factory had not been left untouched long enough.
later_summary.limits: The contestant's instructions in those sessions did not state the hands-off rule, and the required 600 game seconds was an unintended default. The next session, set up on 2026-09-23, states the rule and asks for 60 seconds; it had no recorded result as of 03:52 UTC that day.

later_summary.what: Zach Stern widened the goal: an AI agent plays the game and builds the factory itself, by the game's own rules, from an empty world, observed and assessed as it goes. The test became a ladder of the game's own milestones.

A scripted run, not an AI model, climbed the first stretch of the ladder from an empty world: the parts for milestone 2-1 and for the Space Elevator, then 50 Smart Plating made by an Assembler and delivered.
later_summary.contestant: A fixed script. No model chose its moves.
later_summary.outcome: PASS. The game accepted the delivery and moved from its first phase to the next. Earlier scripted attempts failed and were kept as recorded.
later_summary.limits: The run declared three departures from normal play: a storage box for ore and ingots, 20 extra starting parts to pay for the box, and extra starting fuel. It shows the ladder can be climbed. It does not show that a model can climb it.

later_summary.what: The first AI player on the ladder's first rung, milestone 1-1, choosing every move itself.
later_summary.outcome: Five recorded runs, none earned. In the fifth, 14 of 30 replies held no move, 13 of them because the reply ran out of room while the model was still thinking. That run stopped when its daily budget was spent, with 41 iron ore collected by hand and nothing made by its machines.
later_summary.limits: One model on one rung, with the seat's instructions and tools changing between runs, so this is not a score on a fixed instrument and not a ranking.

later_summary.what: Milestone 1-1 from an empty world, with ore from miners on the map's nodes and every part moved between machines by belt.
later_summary.contestant: A fixed script. No model chose its moves.
later_summary.outcome: PASS, 59 checks of 59. By belt: 324 Iron Plate, 202 Iron Rod and 203 Concrete. The game accepted the milestone payment.
later_summary.limits: Declared hand moves: clearing the rock deposit on each node once, and refuelling the burner. A script run shows the route exists; it does not show a model can take it.

later_summary.what: Milestone 1-2 from an empty world, with a copper line for Wire and an iron line, by belt from miners.
later_summary.contestant: A fixed script. No model chose its moves.
later_summary.outcome: PASS, 52 checks of 52. By belt: 304 Wire, 196 Iron Plate and 170 Iron Rod. In a separate run the same day a burner ran on fuel fed by belt, 28 checks of 28.
later_summary.limits: Declared hand moves: clearing each node once, starting fuel, 48 early Wire carried to pay for the iron line, and the finished Wire carried to the bank once.

later_summary.what: Milestones 1-2 and 1-1 earned in one world that started empty, in a single run.
later_summary.contestant: A fixed script. No model chose its moves.
later_summary.outcome: PASS, 142 checks of 142. By belt: 230 Iron Plate, 190 Iron Rod and 369 Wire for milestone 1-2; 201 Concrete, 342 Iron Plate and 214 Iron Rod for milestone 1-1. No ore, ingot or part was moved by hand after the start.
later_summary.limits: Dated by UTC; it was the evening of 16 November in US Central time, the date the page uses. A further stage that tried to double the iron line built its second machines but the game refused all three power wires, so that stage failed. It was declared outside the run's verdict. This run came before the model run of the same date, listed next.

later_summary.what: Milestone 1-1 earned from an empty world by an AI model that chose every move. The first milestone earned by a model on the ladder.
later_summary.outcome: PASS. The game accepted the payment, and the run record marks it fully earned. Machines the model built made 248 Concrete (200 needed), 128 Iron Plate (100 needed) and 184 Iron Rod (100 needed). Nothing that paid for the milestone was made by hand and no machine was fed by hand. The factory: two Miner Mk1s on an iron node and a stone node, one Smelter, two Constructors, two storage boxes, five belts and one biomass burner. 10 model replies over about 24 minutes, 0.35 US dollars.
later_summary.limits: Dated by UTC; it was the evening of 16 November in US Central time, the date the page uses. One run, not repeated. Declared hand steps: 26 iron ore and 53 limestone mined by hand to clear the two nodes before the miners were placed, not counted toward the cost; 200 biomass put in the burner by hand; finished parts carried by hand from the storage boxes to pay. The model acted through the test's direct building tools, not the fuller command set a contestant will use later. Its first try at a belt to the payment point was refused by those tools. One Constructor made Iron Plate and was then switched to Iron Rod.

later_summary.what: Milestone 1-1 earned from an empty world by a second AI model that chose every move.
later_summary.outcome: PASS. The game accepted the payment, and the run record marks it fully earned. Nothing that paid for the milestone was made by hand and no machine was fed by hand. The test's gateway counted 0.39 US dollars; the provider prices behind that count were not checked, so it is a count and not a bill.

later_summary.what: Milestone 1-2 earned from an empty world by an AI model that chose every move.
later_summary.outcome: PASS. The game accepted the payment, and the run record marks it fully earned. Machines the model built made 175 Iron Plate (150 needed), 213 Iron Rod (150 needed) and 825 Wire (300 needed). No machine was fed by hand. Two Miner Mk1s, six belts and two storage boxes stood at the end. 14 model replies, 68 moves, 0.53 US dollars by the test gateway's count.
later_summary.limits: One run, not repeated, started from an empty world; it does not continue the earlier milestone's world. The model acted through the test's direct building tools, not the fuller command set a contestant will use later. Declared hand steps: 26 iron ore and 22 copper ore mined by hand to clear the two nodes, not counted toward the cost; burner fuel put in by hand; finished parts carried by hand from storage to pay. Its first payment was refused one Wire short; it waited for its machines and paid. Two moves were refused and one failed. The machines were not on level ground: the test's building tool placed some on rocks and cliff faces, tens of metres above or below their neighbours, and reported the asked height to the model, not the built one. The game accepted the belts between them.

later_summary.what: Milestone 1-2 earned from an empty world by a second AI model that chose every move.
later_summary.outcome: PASS. The game accepted the payment, and the run record marks it fully earned. Machines the model built made 198 Iron Plate (150 needed), 151 Iron Rod (150 needed) and 316 Wire (300 needed). No machine was fed by hand. Two Miner Mk1s, six belts and five storage boxes stood at the end. 82 model replies, one move each. The test's gateway counted 0.77 US dollars; the provider prices behind that count were not checked, so it is a count and not a bill.
later_summary.limits: One run, not repeated, started from an empty world; it does not continue the earlier milestone's world. The model acted through the test's direct building tools, not the fuller command set a contestant will use later. Declared hand steps: 21 iron ore and 30 copper ore mined by hand to clear the two nodes, not counted toward the cost; burner fuel put in by hand; finished parts carried by hand to pay, 74 of the Iron Plate straight from a Constructor's output and the rest from storage. Seven moves failed. Each model has one run on this milestone, so the two results are not a ranking. The machines were not on level ground: the test's building tool placed some on rocks and cliff faces, tens of metres above or below their neighbours, and reported the asked height to the model, not the built one. The game accepted the belts between them.

later_summary.what: Milestone 1-3 earned from an empty world by an AI model that chose every move, with most of the Iron Plate handed in made by hand.
later_summary.outcome: PASS by the test's rule. The game accepted the payment, and the run record marks it fully earned. Machines the model built made 134 Iron Plate (100 needed), 356 Screws (300 needed) and 336 Wire (300 needed), and no machine was fed by hand. Three Miner Mk1s, seven belts and four storage boxes stood at the end. 32 model replies, 147 moves, 1.43 US dollars by the test gateway's count.
later_summary.limits: One run, not repeated, started from an empty world; it does not continue the earlier milestone's world. The model acted through the test's direct building tools, not the fuller command set a contestant will use later. The first payment was refused 68 Iron Plate short, because plates the machines had made were spent on belts. The model then made 72 Iron Plate by hand at the bench, which the record marks as not counted as earned, and paid. The test credits the milestone because the machines made more than the cost and its rule lets hand made items pay for buildings; physically, most of the plates handed in were made by hand. Other declared hand steps: 25 iron ore and 30 copper ore mined by hand to clear nodes; burner fuel put in by hand; finished parts carried by hand to pay, 28 of the Iron Plate straight from a Constructor's output. Two moves were refused, 13 failed, and 28 further moves were not run because an earlier move in the same reply failed. The machines were not on level ground: the test's building tool placed some on rocks and cliff faces, tens of metres above or below their neighbours, and reported the asked height to the model, not the built one. The game accepted the belts between them.
